00 · Cold open: At eight o'clock on a Monday morning, in one of the safest cities in the world…
the police could not get out of their own police station.
Their exit was burning. Spikes were spread across the roads. Smoke drifted past the front door.
And a short drive away, in the shadow of a 900-year-old cathedral, men in black were firing into a window.
They fired one hundred and thirteen bullets into one window.
This is the story of that window. Of the men who spent a year trying to break it.
And of what it cost when they finally did.
01 · The City of Money: Stavanger, on Norway's west coast. A small city that struck it rich.
Since the 1970s, oil from the North Sea has made it one of the wealthiest places on the planet.
Where there is money, there is cash. And cash has to be counted somewhere.
That somewhere was NOKAS, Norway's cash-handling service.
Behind these walls, millions of kroner moved every day. They were counted, sorted, sealed and sent out to banks across the region.
The building sat in the middle of town, by the cathedral, the shops and a busy pedestrian street.
Hiding in plain sight was its security. Nobody would dare rob a vault in the middle of the city.
The building's real defence wasn't a gun or a guard. It was glass. Armoured, layered, and built to take punishment.
02 · The Architect: Five hundred kilometres east, in Oslo, a man was making a plan.
He was not the kind of criminal who kicks in a door and hopes for the best. Toska was a planner.
He thought in timelines, routes and minutes.
His target was the NOKAS depot in Stavanger.
The money was guarded by a building, and a building can be beaten. The police, however, can always come. Unless they can't.
So the plan had two halves. One team would break into the depot.
The other team's job was to freeze an entire city's police force in place, for just long enough.
He built a crew of more than a dozen men. Among them was Erling Havnå, later known as the sledgehammer man.
There was Metkel Betew, one of the central figures.
And there was Kjell Alrich Schumann, a name that would come to matter more than any other in this story.
03a · The First Time: Here is the part most people don't know.
The fifth of April was not the first time they came for NOKAS.
Two months earlier, Toska was already inside the courtyard.
3D 1 · Through the Glass: Through the glass, he watched the money being moved away.
03b · Back to the Drawing Board: He had lain in that courtyard, freezing, for nothing.
In court, Toska would later insist it was never an attempt. Only a plan.
Most crews would have walked away. Toska went back to the drawing board.
And he made one assumption that would cost them dearly: that the window was ordinary glass.
All through the late winter of 2004, the gang test-drove their escape route over and over,
from the city centre out to the woods at Sørmarka.
By April, they knew Stavanger's streets better than the people whose job was to protect them.
04a · 5 April 2004: In the early hours of Monday the fifth of April, the pieces moved onto the board.
Weapons, spike strips and smoke grenades were all accounted for.
Stavanger is waking up. None of them know they are standing on the board.
A truck is set on fire across the garage exit. Tear gas is thrown at the main entrance. Spikes are laid across the roads.
In a few moments, Stavanger's police are trapped behind their own doors.
3D 2 · 113: One hundred and thirteen shots. And finally… the glass gives.
04b · Inside the Counting Room: Inside, NOKAS employees watch armed men climb into their workplace.
They are not soldiers. They are people who came to work on a Monday morning.
The robbers demand the money, and they get it:
bag after bag, more than 57 million kroner.
At the time, it was the biggest robbery in Norwegian history.
the plan was already starting to come apart.
05a · The Officer: Not every police officer in Stavanger was trapped behind that burning truck.
Police lieutenant Arne Sigve Klungland was out,
And he was heading toward the gunfire.
05b · Memorial: One of the bullets struck Arne Sigve Klungland in the head.
He died there, in the middle of his own city, on a Monday morning.
06 · Into the Woods: The robbers loaded the money and ran,
along the route they had driven all winter, into the forest at Sørmarka.
Vehicles were swapped and evidence was burned. Within minutes, the men in black dissolved into the trees.
Toska had planned to beat a window, a police station and a city.
He had not planned to kill a police officer. And from this moment, Norway would not rest until every man was found.
07a · The Hunt: What followed became one of the largest criminal investigations in Norwegian history.
That August, The Scream was stolen in Oslo. Some wondered whether it was a distraction.
One photo on the board had no X: David Toska.
He had taken his partner and their one-year-old son, and fled to Spain.
A new life on the Costa del Sol. But he kept using the same email address. The investigators traced it.
07b · Mugshot: Spanish police arrested David Toska in an internet café in Málaga.
One year to the day after the robbery.
08 · The Verdict: On the tenth of March 2006, thirteen men were convicted in Stavanger for the NOKAS robbery.
Together, they were sentenced to a total of one hundred and eighty-one years in prison.
David Toska confessed to the robbery,
but denied firing the fatal shot.
In September 2006, during the appeal at the Gulating Court of Appeal,
Kjell Alrich Schumann was the one who fired the shots that killed Arne Sigve Klungland.
09 · Epilogue: And the money? More than fifty-seven million kroner was taken that morning.
Only around six million has ever been accounted for. The rest, roughly fifty million kroner, has never been found.
The plan took more than a year. The robbery took minutes.
First, they watched through the glass. Then they broke it.
Behind it, they found more money than anyone had ever stolen in Norway. They also lost everything else.
Somewhere out there, fifty million kroner is still missing.
And somewhere in Stavanger, a family still remembers the Monday he went to work… and drove toward the gunfire.
